legacy_report:
SOURCE: "AI Research Preference Models", Thomas Simon Foster (first author, lead with Bassel Al Omari, Tingchen Fu), FAIR at Meta / Oxford, with Foerster and McMilin as equal supervisors. arXiv 2608.13940v2, cs.AI, 25 Aug 2026 (v2). Venue: preprint. Note: the first-author month/year is Aug 2026.
COVERAGE: 32 of 32 pages, about 97k chars. I read the main text, limitations, conclusion, all appendices (A, B, C, D) and skimmed the references. I did not read figure images, only the extracted text and captions. Appendix C text after C.1 was only partly viewed.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- An RPM raises AIRA-dojo's average normalized score on AIRS-Bench from 0.684 (no RPM) to 0.711 (inference-only) and 0.729 (agentic). The oracles are 0.748 (validation) and 0.759 (test).
  number: 0.684 / 0.711 / 0.729 / 0.748 / 0.759
  setup: 20 text and tabular AIRS-Bench tasks, 24 h on one H200, 10 seeds, Qwen3.6-27B for both generator and RPM, Hidden Consistent Evaluation from AIRA 2, 15 candidates per operator step. Agentic RPM used only on Draft and Improve; Debug stays random.
  quote: "both variants beat the unguided baseline's final score of 0.684, with Inference-only reaching 0.711 and Agentic reaching 0.729, narrowing the gap toward the validation-oracle (0.748) and test-oracle (0.759) ceilings."
  where: Sec 5.1, p.6; Fig 2, p.6
- The RPM ranks candidates rather than forecasting scores, because LLMs forecast absolute outcomes unreliably. It is a pairwise knockout tournament over N candidates, given BFS-selected context nodes (up to K non-buggy executed nodes with their validation scores).
  number: none
  quote: "we observed that language models perform unreliably when forecasting absolute metrics or execution outcomes. Consequently, an RPM reformulates experimental allocation as a preference ranking problem"
  where: Sec 3, p.4; Sec 3.3, p.5
- Efficiency: the RPM variants reach the baseline's 24 h score in about 15 h.
  number: 14.88 h (1.61x) inference-only; 15.50 h (1.55x) agentic
  setup: same as above. Only the executed candidate's compute counts toward the 24 h.
  quote: "The Inference-only RPM matches this baseline score in 14.88 hours (a 1.61× speedup), while the Agentic RPM achieves it in 15.50 hours (a 1.55× speedup)."
  where: Sec 5.1, p.7
- Significance is modest. The probability of improvement over no-RPM is about 0.59 for both variants, with the lower 95% CI bounds just above 0.5.
  number: 0.5923 and 0.5913; CI lower bounds 0.5066 and 0.5018
  setup: task-stratified bootstrap using rliable
  quote: "yielding average improvement probabilities of 0.5923 and 0.5913, respectively, with the 95% confidence intervals lower bounded at 0.5066 and 0.5018"
  where: Sec 5.1, p.7
- Selection quality drives the end result: selection advantage (chosen score minus batch mean) correlates with final score.
  number: Pearson r = 0.55 (p = 0.0007), Spearman 0.56 (p = 0.0004)
  setup: one point per seed run (n about 35 by the p-values, not stated)
  quote: "(Pearson r = 0.55, p= 0.0007; Spearman ρ = 0.56, p= 0.0004)"
  where: App C.1, p.29
- Inference-only scaling offline: more context nodes, a bigger candidate pool and more reasoning effort each help.
  number: accuracy 60.7 / 60.9 / 62.7 / 65.0 with growing context (the extraction does not label which context counts go with each number); reasoning effort low 61.3, high 63.4; selection advantage for RPM at n=2/5/10/15 is 0.017/0.030/0.038/0.045 against oracle 0.073/0.141/0.188/0.212
  setup: 1,000 sibling pairs from 40 unreleased image/video/audio tasks, earlier AIRA-dojo runs with gpt-oss-120b, GPT-4o and CWM. Near-ties (gap below 0.01) dropped. Label is the node with the higher best test score in its subtree. Judge is GPT-5. Random is 50%.
  quote: "context scaling demonstrates that supplying the RPM with a deeper history of historical search tree nodes and their validation scores consistently improves child-selection judgment."
  where: Sec 5.2.1, p.7-8; Fig 3, p.8
- Ensembling lifts the judge, and an arbiter that weighs argument quality beats a vote.
  number: GPT-5 64.66, Opus 4.8 67.44, Gemini 3.1 Pro 67.40, majority vote 68.04, LLM arbiter 69.35 (%)
  setup: offline set, max reasoning, 3 rollouts per model
  quote: "A standard majority vote lifts accuracy to 68.04%, but the LLM-Arbiter achieves the top score of 69.35%, showing that weighing the quality of arguments outperforms a simple vote count."
  where: App A.2.3, p.19-20
- Pilot experiments beat pure judgment offline and scale with budget, with diminishing returns.
  number: 78.52% (5 min), 82.78% (30 min), 84.02% (4 h). Fig 5 also prints "validation oracle: 66.73" and "max validation subtree oracle: 90.95".
  setup: offline set, agentic RPM with a sandbox clone including an H200. The end-to-end runs use the 5 min budget.
  quote: "scaling from 78.52% under a 5-minute constraint, to 82.78% at 30 minutes, and peaking at 84.02% with a 4-hour allocation."
  where: Sec 5.2.2, p.8; Fig 5, p.9
- Proxy strategies: agents run reduced-CV or single-split validation and subsample data. Full data is more reliable than subsampling. Removing the LR scheduler or simplifying augmentation hurts accuracy (up to -14.1 pp on one bar). More CV folds don't help because of timeouts. The prompt hints at these proxies, so they are not fully self-discovered.
  where: Sec 5.2.2, p.9; Fig 4-5, p.9
- Ablation design tricks: overstating the time budget (real 300 s, claimed 2700 s, 9x) and a separate feedback model that proposes the next experiment or says stop both help. Removing GPU access causes a significant drop. Without feedback the agent runs many trivial experiments. Loop limits: N=30 experiments, stop threshold 60 s.
  quote: "The real time budget is B = 300s even though we overstate that the time budget is B′ = 2700s, which is 9 times larger than the actual value."
  where: App B.1-B.2, p.22-24; Algorithm 1, p.23; Fig 11-12, p.24
- New SOTA on two tasks.
  number: WinoGrande 94.1% with the agentic RPM (previous agentic SOTA 90.4%); SVAMP 95.7% with inference-only (prior 94.2%)
  quote: "AIRA-dojo with the Agentic RPM achieves an accuracy of 94.1%, comfortably surpassing the previous agentic SOTA of 90.4%"
  where: Sec 5.1, p.7
- Judge reasoning that cites evidence is more accurate. Prior-evidence is 68.3% vs 62.4% when omitted. Correctness is 66.9% vs 63.9%. Pretrained backbone is 67.0% vs 63.9%. Abstract architecture arguments are worse (67.3% down to 64.7%).
  setup: 8,715 pairwise rollouts across 3 LLMs, keyword-matched labels
  where: App A.3, p.20
- Prompt optimization (DSPy MIPROv2, 10 candidates, 40 trials) gave a small gain. It converged on a "Principal Investigator" persona with a 5-criterion rubric that tolerates fixable bugs and penalises redundant directions.
  number: 57.7% to 59.0%
  setup: 990 samples with ties kept
  quote: "The optimized prompt improves selection accuracy from 57.7% to 59.0%."
  where: App A.1.2, p.16
- Judging already-executed nodes (final-node selection) does not beat validation score. Inference-only RPM beats random but degrades as the pool N grows toward 10.
  quote: "validation-based selection enables strong heuristics that are difficult to improve upon purely through code inspection."
  where: App D.3, p.31; Fig 18, p.32

LIMITS (authors)
- LLM inference cost is assumed negligible. Inference-only latency is 0.660 h per 24 h run; adjusted, the score is 0.708 at 23.34 h vs 0.711.
- The offline data comes from greedy runs on different tasks, modalities and backbones, and the subtree-max label is biased. The authors say the main claims therefore rest on the end-to-end results.
- Only the child-creation stage is covered. Final-node selection showed no significant gain. Parent selection is left to future work.
- One scaffold (AIRA-dojo), one backbone (Qwen3.6-27B), one benchmark. "Scaffold-agnostic" is asserted, not shown. The agentic variant needs a sandboxed clone of the environment.
- My observations, not stated by the authors: the oracle ceiling is 0.748 and the gap to the baseline is small. The significance margin is thin. There are no human-taste or open-ended research evaluations. The score is always a benchmark metric, which fits "done reduces to a score" more than "research taste doesn't reduce to a score". The RPM serves to ration the expensive score, not to replace it. The paper does not use the phrase "research taste". Its framing is the "asymmetry of verification" (Wei, 2025): candidates are easy to generate and hard to verify.

BUILDS ON: AIRA-dojo (Toledo et al., 2025); AIRA 2 / Hidden Consistent Evaluation (Hambardzumyan et al., 2026); AIRS-Bench (Lupidi et al., 2026); LLM-as-a-Judge (Zheng et al., 2023); MIPROv2 / DSPy (Opsahl-Ong et al., 2024); ReAct (Yao et al., 2023); rliable (Agarwal et al., 2021); AIDE (Jiang et al., 2025); Zheng et al. (2026), a pairwise predictor of unexecuted ML solutions using static data reports. Goldie et al. (2026) proposed a trained judge for tree-search leaves; the RPM realises this without training. Also cited: Bradley-Terry (1952), RLHF (Christiano 2017), Bayesian optimization / BOHB / early-stopping literature.

CODE: none worth keeping beyond the prompts. The pairwise judge prompt is in Fig 6 (p.16, "You are a strict judge selecting between TWO candidate solutions..."). The optimized PI-persona prompt is in Fig 7 (p.17, "You are a principal investigator allocating compute budget to one of two branches..."). The pilot-loop pseudocode is Algorithm 1 (p.23). The feedback model's JSON schema (stop, reason, next_experiment{title, goal, steps, expected_runtime}) is in Fig 14 (p.26-27).

FIGURES (captions per extraction; I did not view the images)
- Fig 1, p.2: RPM-augmented child creation (select parent, N candidates, RPM picks one, execute only that one). Best single explainer of the loop.
- Fig 2, p.6: score vs compute time and final scores. Shows the agentic RPM starts slow and overtakes later.
- Fig 3, p.8: inference scaling (context, reasoning, pool size vs oracle).
- Fig 4-5, p.9: what the agentic proxy strategies are and which help.
- Fig 11, p.24: ablations.
- Fig 16, p.29: selection advantage vs final score scatter.
- Fig 18, p.32: final-node selection degrades with pool size.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found. The extraction garbled the Limitations bullet 2 (a clause is missing: "the ... biased relative to the online target"). Figure axis values are jumbled in the extraction, so Fig 3 context-count labels are unreliable. The reference list contains 2026 arXiv IDs and models (Claude Opus 4.8, Qwen3.6-27B, Gemini 3.1 Pro) that I could not check. A rough claim count: about 13 claims.
